digest.top_line: ASCO imaging guideline: NGI should be offered when salvage RT is contemplated after RP (evidence high, strong); withhold it when no salvage local therapy is planned.
digest.tldr: A guidance-only day, no trial readouts. Prostate carried most: ASCO ties NGI to a salvage RT decision, an ESTRO ACROP Delphi reached consensus on only 14/40 salvage SBRT items, and an RSS case guide covers intact-prostate SBRT. Gyn: ABS HDR compendium keeps a cervix HR-CTV D90 goal of 85-95 Gy EQD210; ESGO/ESTRO/ESP backs universal MMR/MSI testing.

sites.intro: ABS HDR fractionation reference plus the ESGO/ESTRO/ESP endometrial update; the endometrial source text cuts off before the adjuvant RT grades.

studies.name: ESGO/ESTRO/ESP endometrial carcinoma guidelines
studies.tldr: Joint European guideline update: universal MMR IHC or MSI testing in all EC (III, B); molecular classification needs all four surrogate tests.
details: 🔍 Joint ESGO/ESTRO/ESP update of the 2014 European consensus on endometrial carcinoma
🔍 MEDLINE systematic review, Jan 2014 to June 2019, English only
🔍 Grading uses an adapted IDSA-USPHS system: levels of evidence I-V, grades A-E
🔍 191 external reviewers scored each recommendation for relevance and feasibility

details.text: 📊 Key recommendations captured in source, with level and grade

rows: Multidisciplinary tumor board planning of staging and treatment
Treatment in a specialized center, esp. high-risk or advanced stage
MMR IHC (+ MLH1 promoter methylation) or MSI in all EC, any histology
Genetic counseling if increased Lynch risk
Lynch endometrial surveillance generally from age 35, tailored
Annual TVUS + annual or biennial biopsy until hysterectomy in Lynch carriers
Hysterectomy + BSO after childbearing, preferably before age 40

details.text: 📊 Lynch syndrome cumulative incidence at 70 years by gene

details: 📊 ~3% of all EC and ~10% of MMRd/MSI EC are germline MMR-driven
🔍 Molecular classification needs all four tests: p53, MSH6, PMS2 IHC plus POLE exonuclease-domain sequencing
⚠️ A single surrogate test alone is insufficient: ~5% of carcinomas are 'multiple classifiers'
⚠️ Occult malignancy at prophylactic surgery up to 17% in one retrospective series; counsel before surgery
⚠️ Source excerpt truncates before the adjuvant treatment recommendations; RT-specific grades not reported in source text
studies.significance: The molecular classification is valid only with all four tests (p53, MSH6, PMS2, POLE exonuclease domain), since ~5% of tumors carry multiple classifiers and a single surrogate misassigns them. That classification is reported as prognostic most clearly in high-grade and high-risk tumors, the group where adjuvant decisions are made; the RT recommendations themselves fall outside the captured excerpt.
studies.monday_clinic: In any newly diagnosed endometrial carcinoma, whatever the histologic subtype, this supports MMR IHC or MSI testing to triage Lynch referral (III, B); MMRd alone does not identify a germline carrier, since most cases are sporadic.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Joint **ESGO/ESTRO/ESP** guideline updating the 2014 European consensus. MEDLINE review of **Jan 2014 to June 2019**; recommendations graded on an adapted IDSA-USPHS scale (levels I-V, grades A-E), with **191 external reviewers** and patient input.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **Universal MMR IHC or MSI** in all EC regardless of histology (III, B), with MLH1 promoter methylation testing when MLH1/PMS2 is lost. Lynch surveillance generally **from age 35** and risk-reducing hysterectomy + BSO **preferably before 40** (IV, B).

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The molecular surrogate algorithm (p53, MSH6, PMS2, POLE) is endorsed only as a **complete panel**, because ~5% of tumors are multiple classifiers. POLEmut status requires a pathogenic variant in the **exonuclease domain**.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents women with endometrial carcinoma of any histology and Lynch syndrome mutation carriers. Does not represent heterozygous PMS2 carriers for gynecological surveillance, whose absolute risk the guideline calls very low.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Literature search stopped at **June 2019** and was English-only. The captured excerpt ends before the adjuvant therapy section, so RT and systemic recommendations are not reported in source text.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Molecular classification is prognostic mainly in high-grade and high-risk tumors, the adjuvant-decision group, and is valid only with all four tests. The adjuvant RT recommendations themselves are beyond the captured source text.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Universal MMR IHC or MSI testing serves four roles, including prediction of immune checkpoint inhibitor benefit. Lost MLH1/PMS2 requires promoter methylation testing before germline referral, since most MMRd is sporadic.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Risk-reducing hysterectomy + BSO in Lynch carriers is advised after childbearing, preferably before 40 (IV, B). Occult malignancy at prophylactic surgery reached up to 17% in one retrospective series, so pre-operative counseling and workup carry weight.

studies.name: ABS compendium of gynecologic HDR brachytherapy fractionation
studies.tldr: Cervix HR-CTV D90 goal 85-95 Gy EQD210; no single optimal HDR scheme for any site; doses >7 Gy/fx flagged for higher complication risk.
details: 🔍 ABS Gynecologic Task Force report (2019): literature + prior ABS guidelines + member experience, consensus via conference calls
🔍 Not a systematic review; recommendations made only where the panel agreed
⚠️ Higher dose/fx with fewer fractions raises toxicity; >7 Gy/fx needs optimal implant geometry and OAR review
📊 Cervix EBRT + brachy course to be completed in <7-8 weeks for better local control and survival

details.text: 📊 Target dose goals by setting (EQD210 unless stated)

rows: Inoperable stage I uterine, HDR alone
Inoperable stage I uterine, EBRT + HDR
Post-op vaginal cuff boost after EBRT
65-70 Gy; 70-75 Gy for superficial positive margins

details.text: 📐 OAR D2cc limits: ABS vs EMBRACE-derived (EQD23)
📊 Vaginal cuff brachy alone: most common schemes in the ABS survey, in rank order
💊 Vaginal cuff HDR after EBRT (ABS Table 4)

details: 🔗 Sorbe et al.: the only cited randomized cuff data, 290 pts, 2.5 Gy x 6 vs 5.0 Gy x 6 at 0.5 cm
⚠️ Sorbe arms had equal outcomes but more vaginal shortening at higher dose/fx; low-risk stage IA G1-2 only
🔗 Cervix: 3 x 8 Gy and 2 x 9 Gy are listed as alternatives; an international trial favored 4 x 7 Gy over 2 x 9 Gy for LC
🔍 Interstitial cervix: BID fractions about 6 h apart in one week; Vienna alternative 7 Gy x 4 over two procedures
⚠️ Hybrid IC/IS was needed in about 45% of Vienna pts to reach the D90 goal
⚠️ Vaginal stenosis correlated with rectovaginal reference point EQD23 ≥65 Gy (EMBRACE)
studies.significance: The EMBRACE-derived OAR limits sit below the ABS ones (rectal D2cc ≤65 vs 70-75 Gy, bladder ≤80 vs about 80-90 Gy EQD23), and the panel says lower doses are recommended in practice. For cuff brachy the panel picks no scheme. It flags that 0.5 cm-depth prescriptions need modifying on a 2.5 cm cylinder to keep surface dose acceptable.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **ABS Gynecologic Cancer Task Force** compendium (Brachytherapy 2019). Experts reviewed the literature, the existing ABS guidelines and their own clinical experience, then reached consensus over conference calls. **Not a systematic review.**

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: All schemes are given as **EQD210** for tumor and **EQD23** for OAR, so regimens can be summed and compared. Cervix image-guided target: **HR-CTV D90 85-95 Gy EQD210**, starting from the Point A schedules and then optimized. Interstitial needle loading should hold **no more than 10-20% of total dwell time**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The cervix target range and the tighter OAR limits (**rectal D2cc ≤65 Gy, bladder ≤80 Gy**) come from EMBRACE, not the older ABS 2012 Point A guidance. For the cuff, Portec-2 and institutional series supply the schedules, and Sorbe is the only randomized comparison of fractionation.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents HDR brachy for intact cervix, post-op endometrial cuff, vaginal cancer or recurrence, and medically inoperable stage I uterine cancer. Does not represent LDR or PDR practice, or risk-adapted dose painting beyond HR-CTV, which the authors leave undetailed.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Several of the source tables could not be reliably paired row-to-value here, so specific scheme-to-EQD2 mappings for Point A, interstitial and inoperable uterine schedules are not reproduced. The cervix Point A schedules derive from **2012** ABS guidance and are pre-optimization starting points.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The document is a reference list of what is acceptable, not a ranking. Its practical value is the EQD2 bookkeeping and the explicit caution on **>7 Gy/fx**. It leaves open which cuff scheme is best and how to load newer free-trajectory interstitial applicators.

studies.interpretation:
The most useful way to read this compendium is as a statement of tolerance rather than of optimality. The panel says plainly that no single fractionation scheme is optimal for any gynecologic site. What it actually does is fence the acceptable space: a set of schedules that converge on similar EQD2 values, plus a warning that pushing dose per fraction above 7 Gy buys convenience at the cost of complication risk unless implant geometry and OAR doses are favorable. For a brachytherapist choosing between a three-fraction and a five-fraction cervix course, that framing is more honest than a single recommended regimen would be, because the comparative evidence is thin.

The interesting tension sits between the two generations of dose limits the document carries side by side. The ABS constraints of 70-75 Gy EQD23 for rectum and sigmoid D2cc and roughly 80-90 Gy for bladder are presented next to the lower EMBRACE-derived thresholds (rectal ≤65 Gy, bladder ≤80 Gy), and the authors concede that lower OAR doses are recommended in practice on the strength of the European data. Practically, a planner who treats the ABS numbers as the ceiling is working to an older standard than the panel itself endorses. The same applies to target dose. The 85-95 Gy HR-CTV D90 goal is an image-guided, EMBRACE-anchored target, while the Point A schedules are explicitly labeled pre-optimization starting points. Reaching the upper end of that range for bulky disease required hybrid intracavitary and interstitial technique in about 45% of the Vienna experience, which is a resource statement as much as a dosimetric one.

For the post-hysterectomy cuff, the evidence base is weaker than the table of schedules might suggest. The only randomized fractionation comparison cited (Sorbe, 290 pts, 2.5 Gy x 6 vs 5.0 Gy x 6 to 0.5 cm) enrolled low-risk stage IA grade 1-2 disease, a group in which most current practice would not offer brachytherapy at all, and it found equal outcomes with more vaginal shortening in the higher-dose arm. Everything else rests on institutional series and survey frequency. The most common US scheme, 7 Gy x 3 at 0.5 cm, is therefore a consensus of habit. The point about cylinder diameter is the one most likely to change a plan: a depth prescription that is reasonable on a 3 cm cylinder delivers a materially higher surface dose on a 2.5 cm cylinder, so the prescription should follow the applicator rather than the protocol name.

What would make this document wrong is mainly the passage of time. It was written before newer prospective data on reduced-fraction cervix regimens and modern interstitial applicators matured, and the authors themselves say loading patterns for free-trajectory needles are undefined. The international comparison favoring 4 x 7 Gy over 2 x 9 Gy for local control is a reminder that isoeffective EQD2 arithmetic does not guarantee isoeffective outcomes at the extremes of fraction size. Read it as a floor for safe practice and as an EQD2 lookup, and defer to image-guided dose-volume data where the two disagree.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The EMBRACE-derived OAR limits sit below the ABS ones (rectal D2cc ≤65 vs 70-75 Gy EQD23), and the panel endorses the lower values. For the cuff it names no preferred scheme and flags that depth prescriptions need adjusting on a 2.5 cm cylinder.

open_questions: Optimal vaginal cuff HDR fractionation scheme
Outcomes of 3-fraction vs 4-5 fraction cervix HDR
Loading patterns for newer interstitial applicators

sites.intro: Three guidance documents, all expert opinion or detection data rather than outcome data: NGI before salvage RT post-RP, the unresolved dose and constraint questions in salvage SBRT, and intact-gland SBRT in large or post-TURP prostates.

studies.name: Radiosurgery Society guide to localized prostate SBRT
studies.tldr: Case-based RSS guide to intact-prostate SBRT (≤5 fx): large gland, high baseline IPSS and prior TURP are not contraindications if OAR constraints are met.
details: 🔍 Expert case-based guide endorsed by the Radiosurgery Society; two modified real-world cases, not a trial
🔍 Scope: dose/fractionation, OAR constraints, dose escalation, rectal spacer, ADT with SBRT, high-risk, large prostate, IBD, MR guidance

details.text: 🔍 Case A: unfavorable intermediate-risk, cT1cN0M0, PSA 8.1, 112 mL gland on MRI
subdetails: Neoadjuvant leuprolide 2 mo pre-SBRT → gland 61 mL
Hydrogel spacer, 40 Gy/5 fx QOD to prostate + proximal 1 cm SV, VMAT
6 mo ADT total; IPSS 8 baseline → 10 at 1 yr, PSA ~0.15 after T recovery

details: 🔍 Case B: MR-guided 40 Gy/5 fx with SIB 42 Gy/5 fx to DIL; hip prosthesis artifact less on MRI sim

details.text: 📐 SBRT prescription conventions differ across centers

rows: Covers CTV or PTV, goal 95-99% receiving Rx
Dmax 130-140% of Rx; inhomogeneity deliberately allowed

details: 🔗 Only 5% of PACE-B pts had prostate volume ≥80 mL, so large-gland data are thin
⚠️ One retrospective series found volume ≥50 mL predicted late and any G2+ GU toxicity; others reported favorable toxicity at ≥50-100 mL
⚠️ Authors advise against neoadjuvant ADT solely for cytoreduction, yet Case A used it for that gland
🔗 MIRAGE (NCT04384770) cited as randomized support for MR guidance lowering toxicity
⚠️ Prior TURP data mixed; PACE-B allowed these pts. Recommendations are expert opinion, source truncated
studies.significance: The useful RT detail is the prescription spread: 100% isodose with V105% < 20-30% vs 75-85% isodose with Dmax 130-140%, which makes cross-center dose comparisons unreliable. On gland size, PACE-B had only 5% of pts ≥80 mL, so offering SBRT to large glands rests on retrospective data plus spacer and bladder filling.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with a large prostate, high baseline IPSS or prior TURP, this guide supports offering SBRT with counselling on a harder transient GU flare when OAR constraints are achievable; it does not support neoadjuvant ADT for cytoreduction alone.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Case-based practical guide **endorsed by the Radiosurgery Society**, built on two modified real-world cases. Expert synthesis of existing evidence, not a trial or systematic review.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Both cases **40 Gy in 5 fractions** to prostate + proximal SV; Case B added an MR-guided **SIB of 42 Gy** to the dominant intraprostatic lesion. Case A prescribed to the 100% isodose covering PTV, limiting **V105% (42 Gy) < 20-30%**, with hydrogel spacer and QOD delivery.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: **Large prostate is not a contraindication** if OAR constraints are met; spacer and bladder filling help, and neoadjuvant ADT purely for cytoreduction is discouraged. Pts with baseline IPSS ≥15 had low G3 GU toxicity with prophylactic α1-antagonists but should be counselled on a harder transient flare.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: PACE-B is the reference trial but enrolled few large glands (**5% ≥80 mL**) and allowed prior TURP. MIRAGE (NCT04384770) is cited for MR guidance reducing toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Case A's own neoadjuvant ADT shrank the gland from 112 to 61 mL, so it does not test SBRT on an untreated large gland. Whether large-gland GU risk is specific to SBRT fractionation remains unresolved pending PACE-B subgroup analyses.

studies.interpretation:
This piece is a practical, opinion-based companion to the trials that moved prostate SBRT into standard practice. It is not new evidence. Its value is in naming the decisions where the randomized data run thin and saying, as a society, where the authors would stand. The main example is gland size. PACE-B is the trial most readers lean on, but the guide points out that only 5% of its pts had volumes ≥80 mL, so a radiation oncologist offering SBRT to a 100 mL gland is relying on retrospective series. Those series disagree: one found volume ≥50 mL predicted late and any grade ≥2 GU toxicity, while others reported acceptable toxicity at 50-100 mL with no loss of biochemical control. The guide reads the balance as permissive, conditional on meeting constraints. That is a reasonable judgment, but it is a judgment.

Case A complicates that message. The authors say neoadjuvant ADT should not be used only to shrink the gland, yet the illustrative pt received leuprolide, which took the gland from 112 to 61 mL before SBRT. Unfavorable intermediate-risk disease justifies ADT on oncologic grounds, so the choice can be defended. Still, the case does not show SBRT tolerated by an untreated large gland. A reader looking for reassurance on that exact scenario will not find it here.

The prescription discussion is probably the most transferable part. Prescribing 40 Gy to the 100% isodose with V105% held under 20-30% is a very different dose distribution from prescribing to the 75-85% isodose with Dmax at 130-140%. Single-institution toxicity and control figures are hard to compare without knowing which convention a center uses, and that applies to any dose-escalation claim, including the 42 Gy SIB shown in Case B.

On urinary function, the guide rests its position on retrospective series with generous α1-antagonist prophylaxis in pts with IPSS ≥15. The open question it names is the right one: is the large-gland or poor-baseline GU risk specific to five-fraction delivery, or common to prostate RT of any schedule? The authors point to future PACE-B subgroup analyses for the answer. MIRAGE is cited as randomized support for MR guidance reducing toxicity, which makes MR-guided SBRT a lever for the high-risk-of-toxicity pt rather than only a convenience.

The guide could be wrong if large-gland toxicity turns out to be fractionation-dependent. In that case moderate hypofractionation would be the safer default for these pts, and the permissive stance here would need to narrow. The excerpt was truncated before the high-risk, ADT and IBD sections, so this read covers only the large-gland, baseline urinary and TURP discussion.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Prescription conventions vary widely (100% isodose with V105% < 20-30% vs 75-85% isodose with Dmax 130-140%), so dose comparisons across series need care. Large glands are supported mainly by retrospective data, since PACE-B had only 5% ≥80 mL; spacer, bladder filling and MR guidance (MIRAGE) are the stated mitigations.

open_questions: Is large-gland GU toxicity specific to SBRT fractionation?
Does MR-guided SBRT reduce GU toxicity in large glands?

studies.name: ESTRO ACROP Delphi: salvage SBRT for intraprostatic relapse
studies.tldr: Consensus on only 14/40 items (35%) after 3 Delphi rounds; dose, fractionation, biopsy need and cumulative OAR constraints remain unresolved.
details: 🔍 3-round Delphi, Jul-Dec 2019; 18/33 invited salvage SBRT authors (54.5%), all completed every round
🔍 Consensus defined as >80% agreement; major agreement 65-80%; divided <65%

subdetails: No concomitant ADT with salvage SBRT
Phoenix definition valid for follow-up after re-RT
Primary RT dose factored into salvage dose

details: 📊 Major agreement: ≥2 yr minimum interval from primary RT; dose prescribed to the isodose
📊 Schedules in use: 5-6 fx up to about 35 Gy (30-35 Gy and >35 Gy most frequent)

subdetails: Prior toxicity threshold: 56% exclude after G2+, rest after G3+
Salvage dose higher, lower or same vs primary
Cumulative CTV and OAR dose constraints
Max T, Gleason and PSA for selection

details: ⚠️ Imaging: choline PET 89% vs PSMA-PET 28%; rounds closed before most PSMA-PET data published
⚠️ Panel Europe-weighted: only 2 of 18 from outside Europe (US)
studies.significance: The dosimetric section, at Kendall's W 0.12, is where the panel agreed least: no consensus on salvage dose relative to primary, fractionation, or cumulative rectum/bladder limits. What it does fix is the target and sequencing: focal CTV of mpMRI GTV plus an adaptive margin, no concurrent ADT, and a 2-year minimum interval from primary RT.
studies.monday_clinic: In an M0, ECOG 0-1 man with intraprostatic relapse ≥2 years after primary RT, this expert opinion supports focal SBRT without concurrent ADT as a reasonable option; it does not tell you the dose, fractionation, cumulative OAR limits, or whether imaging alone can stand in for biopsy.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: ESTRO ACROP **Delphi consensus**, 40-item questionnaire in **3 rounds** (Jul 22 to Dec 16, 2019). Items with **>80% agreement** were retired as consensus; an EAU-nominated urologist sat on the reviewing committee.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Panel of **18 of 33** invited authors of salvage SBRT papers (54.5%), all completing every round. **12/18** work in centres treating >2,000 pts/yr; only 2 practise outside Europe.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Consensus on a **focal CTV (mpMRI GTV + adaptive margin)**, dose prescribed to the isodose, and **no concomitant ADT**. Schedules in use were **5-6 fx up to about 35 Gy**, but the panel did not agree on a recommended fractionation or on dose relative to the primary course.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **14/40** items reached consensus (35%), half of them in round 1; consensus or major agreement on **27/40** (68%). Agreement was highest for imaging/staging (W 0.34) and lowest for dosimetry (**W 0.12**).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The Uro-GEC-ESTRO salvage brachytherapy Delphi split on whole-gland vs focal targets and mandated histology; this panel agreed on focal GTV-based CTV but split on biopsy. The Italian AIRO PROLAPSE survey leaned toward concurrent ADT, which this panel rejected.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents intraprostatic relapse after prior definitive prostate RT, metastatic disease excluded, ECOG 0-1. Does not represent prostate-bed recurrence after RP or nodal/distant relapse.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Rounds closed before most PSMA-PET data appeared, so the 28% PSMA-PET endorsement is dated. Panellists were selected as authors of the mostly retrospective, short-follow-up series the consensus draws on, which risks circular endorsement.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The unresolved items (biopsy, dose, cumulative OAR constraints) are the ones a prospective protocol has to fix first. The ongoing trials cited already disagree with each other on interval (2 vs 4 yr) and on whole-gland vs partial CTV.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this document lies less in what the panel agreed on than in where it could not agree. Most of the consensus items describe things a careful radiation oncologist would already do before re-irradiating a prostate: exclude metastatic disease, restrict to ECOG 0-1, do not treat early relapses, and use the Phoenix definition in follow-up. The section that matters most for planning, dose and organs at risk, produced the weakest concordance of the three, with a Kendall's W of 0.12. The panel could not say whether the salvage dose should be higher, lower or equal to the primary course, could not settle on a fractionation, and could not agree on a cumulative constraint for rectum, bladder, femoral heads or penile bulb. Anyone starting a salvage SBRT program will therefore still be choosing those parameters from single-institution experience.

Two positions do carry practical weight. The first is the focal target: CTV defined as the mpMRI GTV plus an adaptive margin. That departs from the Uro-GEC-ESTRO brachytherapy Delphi, which split on whole-gland versus partial targets, and it sits alongside the Corkum systematic review the authors cite, which found no gain in local control or bRFS from whole-prostate re-irradiation and less severe late toxicity with partial re-treatment. The second is the rejection of concurrent ADT, framed explicitly as a way to delay ADT and its quality-of-life cost. The Italian PROLAPSE survey leaned the other way, which shows how far practice varies even within one national community.

Methodology should temper confidence in several ways. The panel was drawn from authors of the salvage SBRT literature, which the discussion itself describes as retrospective with short follow-up; experts endorsing the approach they publish on is a structural bias of this design. The questionnaire was adapted from a brachytherapy instrument and, by the authors' account, built mainly from clinical experience because the data were thin. Timing matters too: the low PSMA-PET endorsement (28% vs 89% for choline PET) reflects rounds that closed before most PSMA-PET detection data were published, so a reader should not take it as a current imaging position.

The biopsy split is the most consequential open question. Guidelines and the MASTER meta-analysis keep histology as the filter against radiological false positives, while only 22% of this panel called biopsy always necessary. The PICTURE data cited (mpMRI avoiding repeat biopsy in 14% with 97% detection of clinically significant disease) were not generated in the post-RT setting, so they support the question rather than answer it. The consensus is a reasonable scaffold for trial eligibility; it is not evidence that salvage SBRT controls disease, which still rests on the retrospective series and the ongoing prospective protocols.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The dosimetric section, at Kendall's W 0.12, is where the panel agreed least: no consensus on salvage dose relative to primary, fractionation, or cumulative rectum/bladder limits. What it does fix is the target and sequencing: focal CTV of mpMRI GTV plus an adaptive margin, no concurrent ADT, and a 2-year minimum interval from primary RT.

open_questions: Optimal salvage SBRT dose and fractionation relative to the primary course
Can PSMA-PET/mpMRI replace biopsy before prostate re-irradiation?
Cumulative OAR constraints for prostate re-irradiation

studies.significance: The only high-evidence, strong recommendation is NGI before contemplated salvage RT after RP (4.4), and Habl et al reported 59% of RT plans changed by 68Ga-PSMA PET/CT. Post-RT rising PSA without salvage intent gets the opposite call (4.5), so imaging should follow the salvage decision, not precede it.
studies.monday_clinic: In post-RP rising PSA with negative conventional imaging where salvage RT is on the table, this supports NGI first; it does not support NGI for men not candidates for, or unwilling to receive, salvage therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: ASCO expert panel with ASTRO, AUA, SNMMI, ACR, SAR and SUO. **Systematic review 2013 to Aug 2018**, 35 studies: 17 systematic reviews ± meta-analysis and 18 primary articles.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Men with advanced prostate cancer: newly diagnosed clinical high-risk, suspected or confirmed metastatic, recurrent, or progressive on treatment, including **nonmetastatic CRPC** and **metastatic CRPC**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: For men in whom **salvage radiotherapy is contemplated**, NGI should be offered (Rec 4.4; evidence high, strength strong). Habl et al reported **59%** RT plan changes from 68Ga-PSMA PET/CT.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Conventional imaging (CT, bone scan, prostate MRI) and/or NGI per scenario. NGI is **not offered** absent salvage intent after RP (4.3) or RT (4.5), and not routinely offered for radiographic progression in mCRPC (4.11).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Evidence is drawn from detection-rate and diagnostic-accuracy meta-analyses of choline, fluciclovine, acetate and 68Ga-PSMA PET. It contains no randomized trial of NGI-guided treatment with clinical outcome endpoints.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents men with advanced prostate cancer where imaging informs salvage or systemic decisions. Does not represent men with no planned change in management, where NGI is advised against.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Literature closes Aug 2018, before the prospective PSMA PET era matured. Much of the recommendation set is **informal consensus** with benefits/harms ratio uncertain.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The guideline makes imaging conditional on a salvage or care-change decision, not a reflex to rising PSA. It does not settle whether NGI-driven stage migration improves outcomes, especially for oligometastatic MDT selection (4.7).

studies.interpretation:
The organizing principle here is that next-generation imaging earns its place only when the result can change what happens next. Nearly every recommendation is gated on intent: offer NGI when salvage radiotherapy or another salvage local therapy is contemplated, and withhold it when no such therapy is planned. That framing is sensible because the evidence base cannot support anything more ambitious. The 35 included studies measure detection rates, sensitivity and specificity, and the proportion of plans changed. None measures whether patients imaged with NGI live longer or stay progression-free longer than those imaged conventionally. A management change is not a benefit until a downstream trial shows it.

For the radiation oncologist, the load-bearing recommendation is 4.4. It is the only one rated high evidence quality with strong strength, and it covers the most common referral: rising PSA after prostatectomy with negative conventional imaging and salvage RT under consideration. The primary data in the review make clear why the panel was confident here: Habl et al reported a changed RT plan in 59% of patients and a changed stage in 43% after 68Ga-PSMA PET/CT. Changing the plan is a statement about target volume and possibly about intent. Whether the extra nodal or distant findings justify extending fields, boosting, or abandoning salvage is exactly what the guideline does not settle.

The asymmetry between the post-prostatectomy and post-radiotherapy scenarios deserves attention. After RT, NGI is supported only when salvage local or regional therapy is contemplated (4.6, intermediate evidence, moderate strength), and is actively discouraged outside a trial when it is not (4.5). That is coherent with the gating principle. It also places the burden on the clinician to decide salvage candidacy before imaging, which in practice often runs in the other direction.

Recommendation 4.7 is the one most likely to age poorly. For hormone-sensitive disease already metastatic on conventional imaging, the panel acknowledges NGI may move a patient from multimodality oligometastatic management to systemic therapy alone. That is stage migration with direct consequences for metastasis-directed RT eligibility, yet the trials defining oligometastatic benefit selected patients on conventional imaging. Applying PSMA-defined burden to thresholds validated on bone scan and CT is a translation the guideline flags only as 'prospective data are limited'.

Vintage is the main reason to read this guideline as a floor rather than a ceiling. The search closes in August 2018, and PSMA ligands appear 'where available', listed alongside choline and fluciclovine rather than above them. A reader applying it now should treat the scenario gating as durable and the tracer hierarchy as superseded. The castration-resistant recommendations (4.8 to 4.11) rest on weak or insufficient evidence and largely defer to conventional imaging and the PCWG3 principle that PSA progression alone should not drive a therapy change.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Rec 4.4 (high evidence, strong) backs NGI before salvage RT after RP, with 59% RT plan changes and 43% stage changes in Habl et al. For post-RT BCR, NGI is supported only when salvage local or regional therapy is contemplated (4.6, moderate).
significance_by_specialty.medonc: In metastatic CRPC, PSA progression alone should not drive a therapy switch, and conventional imaging stays the serial comparator (4.9, strong). In nonmetastatic CRPC, NGI is reserved for when a care change is contemplated (4.8), and evidence is weak.

papers.abstract: PURPOSE Provide evidence- and expert-based recommendations for optimal use of imaging in advanced prostate cancer. Due to increases in research and utilization of novel imaging for advanced prostate cancer, this guideline is intended to outline techniques available and provide recommendations on appropriate use of imaging for specified patient subgroups. METHODS An Expert Panel was convened with members from ASCO and the Society of Abdominal Radiology, American College of Radiology, Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging, American Urological Association, American Society for Radiation Oncology, and Society of Urologic Oncology to conduct a systematic review of the literature and develop an evidence-based guideline on the optimal use of imaging for advanced prostate cancer. Representative index cases of various prostate cancer disease states are presented, including suspected high-risk disease, newly diagnosed treatment-naïve metastatic disease, suspected recurrent disease after local treatment, and progressive disease while undergoing systemic treatment. A systematic review of the literature from 2013 to August 2018 identified fully published English-language systematic reviews with or without meta-analyses, reports of rigorously conducted phase III randomized controlled trials that compared ≥ 2 imaging modalities, and noncomparative studies that reported on the efficacy of a single imaging modality. RESULTS A total of 35 studies met inclusion criteria and form the evidence base, including 17 systematic reviews with or without meta-analysis and 18 primary research articles. RECOMMENDATIONS One or more of these imaging modalities should be used for patients with advanced prostate cancer: conventional imaging (defined as computed tomography [CT], bone scan, and/or prostate magnetic resonance imaging [MRI]) and/or next-generation imaging (NGI), positron emission tomography [PET], PET/CT, PET/MRI, or whole-body MRI) according to the clinical scenario.
